cards.statement: BigQuery can reduce cross-slot shuffling by storing parent-child data in nested and repeated fields.
cards.explanation: Nested and repeated fields keep frequently queried hierarchical data together within execution slots. This reduces the coordination needed to join separate parent and child tables.

cards.statement: BigQuery fills _PARTITIONTIME with the source event timestamp for a late-arriving row by default.
cards.explanation: BigQuery uses ingestion time for default ingestion-time partition placement. A delayed event follows its arrival time even when its application timestamp points to an older event.
cards.misconception: Ingestion-time partitioning automatically groups delayed records by when their source events occurred.

cards.statement: BigQuery can use a scalar subquery reading another table as the constant needed for partition pruning.
cards.explanation: A partition comparison against a value read from another table is dynamic. BigQuery needs a constant filter expression to determine eligible partitions before reading table data.
cards.misconception: A scalar subquery supplies a constant for partition pruning because it returns one value.

cards.statement: BigQuery requires an eligible partition filter when a view reads a table with that requirement.
cards.explanation: A view keeps the base table's partition-filter requirement. The view definition or its calling query needs an eligible predicate for partition elimination.

cards.statement: BigQuery clustering narrows block reads for selective filters on columns containing many distinct values.
cards.explanation: High-cardinality clustering gives BigQuery detailed metadata about where matching values reside. Selective queries use that metadata to skip irrelevant storage blocks.

cards.statement: BigQuery lets a later clustering column take sorting precedence over an earlier column in the same definition.
cards.explanation: BigQuery sorts clustered data in the declared column order, with earlier columns taking precedence. Filters beginning with the leading columns best match that storage layout.
cards.misconception: Clustering gives its columns independent sorting precedence, like separate indexes.

cards.statement: BigQuery combines cached results with appended rows when it incrementally updates a single-table materialized view.
cards.explanation: Eligible single-table materialized views reuse their stored result after appends to the base table. BigQuery processes the additions and combines them with that result.

cards.statement: BigQuery limits smart tuning to queries that explicitly reference the chosen materialized view.
cards.explanation: Smart tuning rewrites eligible base-table queries to use a matching materialized view. The query author can keep the original base-table references.
cards.misconception: Using a materialized view for acceleration requires rewriting query text to name the view.

cards.statement: BigQuery can use a search index to accelerate equality filters comparing indexed strings with literals.
cards.explanation: Search indexes also serve supported equality predicates on string columns. The optimizer uses the index when it expects a benefit.

cards.statement: BigQuery verifies declared primary-key constraints before using them to eliminate query joins.
cards.explanation: BigQuery trusts declared key constraints during optimization and leaves their enforcement to the data owner. Violating them can produce incorrect query results.
cards.misconception: The optimizer checks actual uniqueness before trusting a declared primary key.

cards.statement: BigLake tables use a connection's service account to read the external files queried by a user.
cards.explanation: A BigLake table delegates external file access to its connection's service account. Query users receive table permissions instead of needing permission to read the underlying files.

cards.statement: BigQuery Storage API connectors bypass a BigLake table's column access policies when Spark reads its data.
cards.explanation: The BigQuery Storage API enforces BigLake table access policies for connector reads. Spark receives data subject to the table's row and column controls.
cards.misconception: Reading through an open-source engine's connector bypasses BigLake table governance.

cards.statement: BigQuery lets a SQL DELETE remove rows from an object table that references Cloud Storage files.
cards.explanation: BigQuery object tables are read-only metadata indexes over Cloud Storage objects. BigQuery rejects DML operations that delete their rows.
cards.misconception: Object table metadata rows support the same SQL deletions as standard BigQuery table rows.

cards.statement: Apache Iceberg managed tables in BigQuery keep their data files in a customer-owned Cloud Storage bucket.
cards.explanation: BigQuery manages Apache Iceberg managed tables while storing their data in customer-owned buckets. This combines managed table operations with customer control of the storage location.

cards.statement: BigQuery automatically tracks new snapshots for an Iceberg external table linked to a JSON metadata file.
cards.explanation: An Iceberg external table created from a JSON metadata file stays tied to that file. Engineers update the table definition to point at newer snapshot metadata.
cards.misconception: A JSON-backed Iceberg external table follows new metadata snapshots automatically.

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog can link custom lineage to catalog entries by matching their fully qualified names.
cards.explanation: Engineers submit custom lineage through the Data Lineage API. Matching fully qualified names connect that lineage to corresponding Knowledge Catalog entries, including entries for on-premises sources.

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog automatically applies an access group's default IAM role to supported data product assets.
cards.explanation: A data product owner assigns a default IAM role to an access group. Knowledge Catalog applies that role across supported assets, reducing per-asset permission configuration.

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog data profile scans replace null source values with the scanned column's mean.
cards.explanation: Knowledge Catalog data profile scans report statistics such as null percentages and numeric averages. They describe the source data rather than impute missing values into it.
cards.misconception: A profiling scan uses its computed statistics to clean the source table.

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog can group assets from different Google Cloud locations into one data product.
cards.explanation: A Knowledge Catalog data product and its underlying assets reside in the same Google Cloud location. Location therefore constrains which assets a producer packages together.
cards.misconception: A data product groups assets across locations regardless of where those assets reside.
cards.volatilityNote: Data product location restrictions may change as supported assets and governance capabilities expand.

cards.statement: BigQuery can reject an on-demand query before execution when estimated bytes exceed its maximum bytes billed.
cards.explanation: BigQuery checks the estimated bytes against maximum bytes billed before running an on-demand query. Exceeding the threshold fails the query before it incurs a query charge.

cards.statement: BI Engine memory reservations apply to queries running in the reservation's project and location.
cards.explanation: A BI Engine reservation assigns memory to a project in a specific location. Dashboards querying another location need capacity there rather than drawing from the original reservation.

cards.statement: BI Engine can accelerate tables outside its preferred tables list when the reservation has spare memory.
cards.explanation: A BI Engine preferred tables list limits acceleration to that set. Queries against other tables use regular BigQuery slots even when the BI Engine reservation has spare memory.
cards.misconception: Preferred tables receive priority while unused BI Engine memory remains available for other tables.

cards.statement: BigQuery can serve a direct materialized-view query from its last refresh within the max_staleness interval.
cards.explanation: For a direct query, max_staleness permits BigQuery to reuse a materialized view's cached result while its refresh lies within that interval. This trades fresher dashboard data for lower latency.

cards.statement: BigQuery uses an authorized view's grant on the source dataset to read data for the view's consumers.
cards.explanation: The source dataset grants access to the authorized view. Consumers receive access to the view, so it exposes its query result while source-table IAM permissions stay separate.

cards.statement: BigQuery can combine granted row-level access policies by intersecting their filters for the same user.
cards.explanation: BigQuery combines the rows granted by a user's row-level access policies as a union. A row is visible if it satisfies a policy that grants that user access.
cards.misconception: A user covered by multiple row-level access policies sees the intersection of their granted rows.

cards.statement: BigQuery can enforce policy-tag read permissions on destination columns for the Storage Write API (gRPC).
cards.explanation: The Storage Write API (gRPC) skips destination policy-tag read checks. BigQuery verifies table write permission; reading protected columns uses separate access checks.
cards.misconception: Streaming inserts need read permission on policy tags protecting destination columns.

cards.statement: BigQuery can apply dynamic data masking through a data policy assigned directly to a table column.
cards.explanation: A BigQuery column can reference a data policy carrying its masking rule. That direct assignment removes the need to organize the rule through a policy-tag taxonomy.

cards.statement: BigQuery stage metrics with compute maximum well above compute average can signal uneven data distribution.
cards.explanation: A BigQuery stage's high maximum compute time relative to its average points to workers doing unequal amounts of work. Engineers inspect the data distribution to investigate skew.

cards.statement: Data Studio directly queries an extracted data source's original system when it renders a report.
cards.explanation: A Data Studio extracted data source holds a stored snapshot. Source changes appear after the extract is updated manually or on its configured update schedule.
cards.misconception: Report rendering reads the original source behind an extract instead of its stored snapshot.

cards.statement: Connected Sheets computes a BigQuery pivot table's aggregates from the rows displayed in its preview.
cards.explanation: Connected Sheets runs pivot-table analysis against the full connected BigQuery data. The sheet's limited preview changes what the user sees in the preview, rather than the source rows used for aggregation.
cards.misconception: The preview row subset is the input for connected pivot-table aggregation.

cards.statement: BigQuery ML automatically reapplies a model's TRANSFORM preprocessing when predicting from new input data.
cards.explanation: A model's TRANSFORM clause preserves its preprocessing pipeline, including learned transformation statistics. BigQuery ML uses the same transformations on prediction inputs.

cards.statement: BigQuery ML automatically standardizes numeric features during boosted tree model training.
cards.explanation: BigQuery ML leaves numeric features unstandardized in its automatic preprocessing for boosted tree models. Tree models are exceptions to the numeric standardization used for many other model types.
cards.misconception: BigQuery ML applies the same automatic numeric standardization to boosted trees as to many other models.

cards.statement: ML.EVALUATE reports training-set metrics by default for a built-in BigQuery ML classifier with a held-out split.
cards.explanation: For a built-in classifier with a held-out split, BigQuery ML evaluates against held-out data. ML.EVALUATE with omitted input returns these saved metrics rather than scoring the fitted training rows.
cards.misconception: ML.EVALUATE's default metrics describe the rows used to fit a classifier even when training reserved a held-out split.

cards.statement: BigQuery ML remote models can run endpoint inference on BigQuery slots allocated to the prediction query.
cards.explanation: BigQuery ML remote models send input data to a model hosted on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The platform performs inference; BigQuery calls the endpoint and receives its predictions.
cards.misconception: A BigQuery ML remote model executes its model computation on BigQuery slots because prediction starts from a BigQuery query.

cards.statement: BigQuery ML can automatically reload an imported TensorFlow model when its files in Cloud Storage change.
cards.explanation: BigQuery ML freezes an imported TensorFlow model when it creates the model. Later edits to its Cloud Storage source files leave that imported model unchanged.
cards.misconception: An imported TensorFlow model remains a live link to its source files and refreshes after those files change.

source.title: The CREATE MODEL statement for importing TensorFlow models

cards.statement: Feature Store on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform can use BigQuery tables or views as its offline store.
cards.explanation: Feature values and their history stay in BigQuery tables or views. Feature Store on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform uses these sources instead of provisioning a separate offline data store.
tags: Feature Store on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

source.title: About Feature Store on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

cards.statement: BigQuery ML requires reserved capacity for imported TensorFlow inference on images in object tables.
cards.explanation: Running an imported TensorFlow model against image object tables uses capacity-based pricing through reservations. BigQuery excludes on-demand pricing for this inference path.
cards.volatilityNote: Supported pricing and reservation requirements for object-table inference can change.

source.title: Run inference on image object tables

cards.statement: Google recommends AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING over ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING for new BigQuery embedding queries.
cards.explanation: AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING provides the same functionality as ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING with simpler output column names. Google's guidance favors AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING for new queries.
cards.volatilityNote: BigQuery AI function names and recommendations change frequently.

cards.statement: BigQuery VECTOR_SEARCH guarantees exact nearest-neighbor results when its query uses a vector index.
cards.explanation: VECTOR_SEARCH uses approximate nearest neighbor search when it uses a vector index. Searching fewer candidates trades recall for speed, so it can miss an exact nearest neighbor.
cards.misconception: A vector index accelerates VECTOR_SEARCH while guaranteeing the same nearest-neighbor results as an exact search.

cards.statement: BigQuery can automatically refresh a vector index in the background after the indexed table changes.
cards.explanation: BigQuery maintains vector indexes asynchronously as the indexed table changes. New rows can take time to appear in the index because refresh runs in the background.
